text:
For two years I tried to write before work. I managed it maybe nine times.

Then I stopped trying to write and started doing something smaller: open the document, read the last paragraph, close it. That was the whole commitment. Ninety seconds.

I didn't get more disciplined. I got a lower barrier.

Within a month I was writing most mornings — not because opening the file was magic, but because it removed the decision. There was nothing to negotiate with at 6am. No motivation required, because nothing hard was being asked yet.

Most of what we call procrastination is a task that's too big to start, not a person too weak to try. Motivation gets you through the first week. The size of the first step gets you through the year.

What's the smallest version of the thing you keep putting off?

The Stopwatch Trap: What Frederick Taylor Got Right — and Wrong

In medical device service, we love a clean metric. First-time fix. Time on site. Tickets closed per tech per week.

This is Scientific Management Theory — Frederick Taylor's idea that work should be studied, measured, and standardized into the one best way to do it.

He wasn't wrong about the value of that:

• A documented install checklist means the tenth laser goes in like the first.

• A standard parts kit turns a two-visit repair into one.

• A defined training script means every provider leaves confident, not guessing.

Standardization is a gift. It protects the customer from our worst day.

But Taylor measured the task and forgot the human holding the tool.

A tech who beats the clock and leaves a nervous injector behind hasn't won anything.

Speed closes a ticket. Presence keeps an account.

What if we measured the one best way to do the work — and then protected the ten extra minutes that make people stay?

Standards create consistency.

Judgment creates loyalty.

Where does your team need more standard work — and where do they need more room?

The Peak-End Rule: Why the Last Five Minutes Decide the Account

In medical aesthetics, we obsess over the middle of the service call. The diagnostics. The parts. The fix.

But ask a practice manager what they remember about a visit and they won't describe the middle at all.

This is the Peak-End Rule. In plain terms, people judge an experience by its best moment and its final moment, not by the average of everything in between.

So the ending is not a formality:

• Fixed the handpiece but left without walking the injector through a test pulse? They remember uncertainty.

• Ran four hours long but ended with a clear summary and a direct number? They remember being looked after.

• Cleaned the room, restacked the cart, said thank you by name? That's the peak they'll repeat to their rep.

The reverse holds too. A flawless repair can be erased by a rushed goodbye.

Every visit has a last impression. Most are accidental.

What if your team designed the final five minutes as deliberately as the first diagnostic step?

The repair earns the ticket.

The goodbye earns the renewal.

How does your team close out a call?

The Service Recovery Paradox: Why Your Worst Day Can Win the Account

In medical aesthetics, we treat a complaint like damage. Something to contain, log, and move past quietly.

But the accounts that renew hardest are rarely the ones that never had a problem.

This is the Service Recovery Paradox. In plain terms, a customer who has a failure fixed brilliantly often ends up more loyal than a customer who never had a failure at all.

Why? Because nothing else in the relationship proves you will show up.

• Device down on a Friday with a full book? Getting a loaner in before Monday is worth more than a year of quiet uptime.

• Shipped the wrong applicator? Owning it in one call, no blame, no maze, is remembered longer than the error.

• Training didn't land and treatments are inconsistent? A second session, unbilled, buys you three years.

The opposite is true too. A slow, defensive recovery erases a decade of good service.

Silence loses accounts. Delay compounds them.

Speed and ownership rebuild them.

What if your team treated every escalation as a retention opportunity, not a failure report?

Prevention protects the contract.

Recovery earns the relationship.

How does your team respond in the first hour after something goes wrong?

The Peak-End Rule: Clients Don't Remember the Average

In medical device service, a visit can go well for six hours and still score poorly. We look at the survey and blame the survey.

It isn't the survey. It's memory.

This is the Peak-End Rule. In plain terms, people store an experience as two snapshots: the highest point and the last point. The rest fades.

So the shape of the visit matters more than the length of it.

If the tech solves a problem the practice didn't even report? That's the peak.

If the install runs late but ends with the injector treating confidently on her own device? That's the peak.

If the paperwork is signed in the hallway on the way out the door? That's the ending they keep.

If the last words are "someone will follow up"? That's the ending they repeat.

The reverse deserves attention too. A visit with no peak and no ending is forgettable, and forgettable accounts shop around.

Good work is the floor. Memory is built on purpose.

What if every visit had one planned high point and one planned close?

Competence keeps you in the building.

Memory keeps you in the contract.

What is the peak moment your team creates on purpose?

The Service Recovery Paradox: The Audition Nobody Asks For

In medical device service, we assume trust is built on the days everything works. It isn't. Trust is built on the day it doesn't.

This is the Service Recovery Paradox. In plain terms, a customer whose problem is handled brilliantly often trusts you more than a customer who never had a problem at all.

A clean record proves nothing. It only means you haven't been tested yet.

If a part is backordered? Then call before they notice, with a date and a plan.

If a tech misses the window? Then the manager calls, not the scheduler.

If an install slips two weeks? Then protect their launch date, not your excuse.

If you billed them wrong? Then fix it in one email, no forms.

The opposite holds too. A quiet, technically perfect year builds a relationship no deeper than the contract it sits on.

Perfection is invisible. Recovery is unforgettable.

One is expected. One is earned.

What if your team stopped hiding the bad days and started using them?

Uptime keeps you competitive.

Recovery keeps you chosen.

What was the last problem your team turned into a reason to stay?

The Peak-End Rule: We Budget for the Welcome and Improvise the Goodbye

In medical device, the arrival is designed. Welcome kit, kickoff call, install agenda, a named contact.

The departure gets whatever minutes are left in the day.

This is the Peak-End Rule. In plain terms, people store an experience by its strongest moment and its final moment, and almost nothing else survives.

Which means the exit is doing more work than the intro:

• A phone support call that ends with "try that and let me know" leaves them holding the problem.

• A training day that ends with a printed protocol and one saved contact leaves them capable.

• A tech who leaves while the room is still a mess hands the practice a chore, not a fix.

• A de-install done with the same care as the install is why they buy the next platform from you.

The reverse is worth sitting with. A strong start with a vague ending reads as abandonment, no matter how good the middle was.

Beginnings set expectations.

Endings set memory.

One is marketing. One is retention.

What if the last five minutes had an agenda, the same way the first five do?

A good welcome opens the account.

A good goodbye keeps it.

What does your team's exit ritual actually look like today?

Goodhart's Law: The Day First-Time-Fix Stopped Telling the Truth

In medical device service, first-time-fix is one of the best numbers we have. Then we put it on a dashboard, tie it to a bonus, and it quietly stops being true.

This is Goodhart's Law. In plain terms, when a measure becomes a target, people optimize the measure instead of the thing it was meant to represent.

Watch how it shows up:

• A tech marks the call resolved, then books a "new issue" ticket next week for the same handpiece.

• A hard fault gets swapped instead of diagnosed, because parts cost less than a second visit on the scorecard.

• A practice is told it's operator error, and the number stays clean while the account gets colder.

• Response time looks great because someone drove out to say the part hasn't shipped.

The opposite is worth noticing too. Teams that talk about the outcome tend to hit the number anyway.

Metrics describe health. They don't create it.

Measure the wrong thing and you get exactly that.

What if your review meetings asked what actually happened for the customer before asking what the number did?

Targets drive behavior.

Purpose drives the right behavior.

Which metric on your team's board is being managed instead of earned?

The Trust Equation: The Rep Who Pushes Least Often Wins the Account

In medical aesthetics, we coach urgency. Ask for the close, create the deadline, get the signature before the quarter ends.

Then we watch a quieter competitor take the account.

This is the Trust Equation. In plain terms, trust equals credibility plus reliability plus intimacy, all divided by self-orientation. Whatever you gain in the top, you lose faster in the bottom.

Which is why the math punishes hunger:

• Credibility is knowing the treatment settings, not just the spec sheet.

• Reliability is the callback you promised on Tuesday arriving on Tuesday.

• Intimacy is knowing the practice is short one injector this month, and planning around it.

• Self-orientation is bringing the upgrade quote to a room that is still frustrated about last week's downtime.

The opposite deserves a look too. A rep with average product knowledge and zero agenda often outlasts the expert who needs something.

Hunger reads as pressure.

Patience reads as partnership.

One closes a deal. One keeps a customer for a decade.

What if every field visit had a version with nothing to sell in it?

Selling asks for a decision.

Trust makes the decision obvious.

Where does your team's self-orientation quietly show up?

The Zeigarnik Effect: The Open Ticket Lives Rent Free in Their Head

In medical aesthetics, a clinic will forgive a broken laser. What they won't forgive is not knowing where things stand.

This is the Zeigarnik Effect. In plain terms, the brain keeps unfinished tasks active and nagging, and drops them the moment they're closed.

So an open ticket is not paperwork. It's a background process running in your customer's head.

• A part ordered with no ETA gets checked ten times before it ships.

• A ticket "escalated to engineering" with no owner becomes a story the practice tells other practices.

• A credit promised verbally stays open until it shows on an invoice.

• A training question answered with "I'll find out" is remembered long after the answer arrives.

The opposite is true too. A clear close, even a close they don't love, ends the loop. A dated no beats an undated maybe.

Silence feels like drift.

Drift feels like risk.

Risk gets a second quote.

What if closing loops was treated as a retention activity, not admin cleanup?

Speed solves the machine.

Closure calms the customer.

How many loops is your team leaving open this week?

Loss Aversion: Clinics Fear a Dark Room More Than They Want a New Feature

In medical aesthetics, we build the pitch around what's new. Faster treatment times, a new handpiece, a better interface.

The practice nods, then asks what happens if it goes down on a Friday.

This is Loss Aversion. In plain terms, people feel a loss about twice as strongly as they feel an equal gain.

Which changes what your team should actually be selling:

• A booked room that goes dark for three days is real money out the door, and they can name the number.

• A rescheduled patient is not just revenue, it's a patient who books somewhere else next time.

• An injector idle for an afternoon is payroll spent on nothing.

• A new feature is a maybe. Downtime is a memory they already have.

The reverse is worth naming too. Practices rarely churn because a competitor had better specs. They churn because they lost days.

Features win attention.

Protection wins signatures.

Uptime is the product.

What if your team led with loaner terms, response commitments, and parts stocking before slide three?

Upgrades sell excitement.

Uptime sells peace of mind.

What does one lost treatment day actually cost your customers, and can your team say it out loud?

The Endowment Effect: Why They Defend the Device They Learned On

In medical aesthetics, we assume a better platform sells itself. Then a practice fights to keep the ten year old system with the sticky footswitch.

This is the Endowment Effect. In plain terms, people value something more once they own it, simply because it's theirs.

And ownership is not the invoice. It's the hours they put in.

• The protocol they tuned themselves feels safer than the one in your manual.
• The button sequence they teach new injectors is now house knowledge, not settings.
• The macro someone built for a favorite treatment is a small act of authorship.
• The old unit in room three has patient outcomes attached to it, and stories.

The reverse matters just as much. Every trade-in, software update, and workflow change asks them to hand back something they built.

So it reads as loss, not progress.

Resistance is rarely stubbornness.

It's attachment you helped create.

What if your team named what the practice keeps before explaining what changes?

Deepen ownership and you earn loyalty.

Dismiss ownership and you earn resistance.

Where is your team asking a customer to give up something they authored?

Diffusion of Innovation: The Same Install, Five Different Clinics

In medical aesthetics, we roll out a new platform with one install plan, one training deck, and one follow-up cadence. Then we wonder why two clinics are booking full days by week two and three are still using it once a week.

This is Diffusion of Innovation. In plain terms, new technology spreads through a population in stages, and each group needs a different reason to move.

So read the room before you standardize the support:

• Innovators want access. Give them beta settings and treat their feedback as real input.

• Early adopters want an edge. Give them protocols, marketing angles, and a case to present.

• The early majority wants proof. Give them another practice's numbers, not your spec sheet.

• The late majority wants safety. Give them a checklist, a named contact, and a second training visit.

• Laggards want their old workflow back. Give them one small win, then build.

The opposite trap is real too. Support your laggards like innovators and they stall. Support your innovators like laggards and they disengage.

Adoption is not a launch date.

It's a curve.

What if your install plan had five versions instead of one?

Training teaches the device.

Matching the customer creates utilization.

Where on the curve does your team's toughest account actually sit?
